Its four-by-four pressure-sensitive pads have become a common interface in DJ technology. DJ Shadow made a work built entirely of samples on the MPC60 MKII; J Dilla switched off quantisation and arrived at a sampled style that drifts off the beat; Kanye West wrote several well-known tracks on an MPC and performed the track Runaway on an MPC2000XL at the MTV Video Music Awards.

The case is mostly black or silver plastic, built to be sturdy and durable for stage and studio use.

The Akai MPC is a music workstation that the Japanese company Akai has brought out since 1988; it is an electrophone, used mainly in electronic music, hip-hop production and the modern studio. Its core is a 4x4 grid of pressure-sensitive rubber pads combined with sampling and sequencing: the user can record a sound fragment, edit it, assign it to a pad, and then trigger it like a keyboard or a drum kit to build a rhythm. The interface was simplified compared with earlier equipment, and it can be connected to an ordinary sound system. Well-known users include DJ Shadow, J Dilla and Kanye West, and its pad interface has become a common standard in DJ technology.
Akai MPC由Akai與Roger Linn合作，1988年推出MPC60，: The Akai MPC was a collaboration between Akai and Roger Linn: the MPC60 came out in 1988, followed by the MPC60 MkII and the MPC3000. Its velocity-sensitive pads simplified sampling and sequence arranging, and it influenced electronic and hip-hop music, becoming a standard of DJ technique. In 2006 Akai collapsed and its assets were bought by Numark, and Akai continues to bring out new models. Users such as DJ Shadow, J Dilla and Kanye West created work on it, and J Dilla's MPC is held by the National Museum of African American History and Culture in the United States.
Akai MPC的音色特徵取決於所載入的取樣音源，具有高度的可塑性與多樣性。其音: The timbre of the Akai MPC depends on the samples loaded into it, so it is highly plastic and varied. Its sound is usually clear and directly digital, carrying the texture of the original samples. The range is very wide, from low drum sounds to high voices. The MPC shapes resonance by layering several samples and by adjusting pitch and filtering, creating a rich sense of space. Against the organic warmth of traditional instruments the MPC sounds more modern and more electronic; against a synthesiser, because it uses real recorded material directly, it feels more familiar and more recognisable. Its character sits between the real instrument and the electronic synthesiser: it keeps the warmth of the original sound while bringing the precision and creative potential of digital processing.
